--- title: "Scattered data" engine: julia --- ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` rms (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: Measurements rarely come on a grid. The Julia package handles scattered points by fitting a grid to them: a convolution interpolant on a grid over the points' bounding box, whose knot values are chosen so that the interpolant matches the points. The result is an ordinary gridded interpolant, so everything on the other pages — evaluation anywhere, derivatives, integrals — works on it unchanged. `fit_scattered` does the fit and returns the grid; `convolution_interpolation(points, values)` does the fit and returns the interpolant. The Python port does not include scattered data yet; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd) tracks the port. ## Two modes - `mode = :smooth`, the default, smooths: it minimises the misfit at the points plus a roughness penalty whose weight is chosen by generalized cross-validation, and reports the noise level it found. For measured data, which carry noise. - `mode = :exact` interpolates: the fit passes through every point to machine precision, and among the grids that do, the smoothest is chosen. For trusted, noise-free data only — noise would be reproduced exactly and amplified between the points. The default differs from the gridded constructors, which always interpolate, because scattered data are usually measurements. ## Noisy measurements Points in the unit square, one per column of the matrix, with a smooth signal and noise: ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Random.seed!(1) # reproducible points and noise pts = rand(2, 800) # 800 scattered points in 2D, one per column signal(x, y) = sin(3x) * cos(2y) # the signal σ = 0.05 # the noise standard deviation vals = [signal(p[1], p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts)] # the signal at the points noisy = vals .+ σ .* randn(800) # measured with noise knots, grid, info = fit_scattered(pts, noisy) # the fitted grid, smoothing chosen by cross-validation itp = convolution_interpolation(knots, grid; kernel = :a4, bc = :poly) # the interpolant, with the kernel the fit used info # the smoothing parameter and the estimated noise ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (lambda = 4.468668507024199e-9, noise = 0.0499329936234454) ``` ::: ::: | | the noisy points | the fitted interpolant | |:--|--:|--:| | rms error against the signal | 0.0501 | 0.0116 | | | generated | estimated by the fit | |:--|--:|--:| | noise standard deviation | 0.0500 | 0.0499 | ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The grid is sized from the point density, as fine as the points resolve, and the smoothing is set by the penalty weight, not by the knot count; the [smoothing page](smoothing.qmd) compares this fit with Gaussian smoothing on gridded data. ## Trusted data With `mode = :exact` the interpolant passes through the points. Since it is a gridded interpolant underneath, its derivatives and integrals come from the same object; the wrapper forwards `derivative`, so a box integral over the points' domain is four evaluations of the twofold antiderivative: ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Random.seed!(2) pts2 = rand(2, 300) # 300 trusted points vals2 = [signal(p[1], p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts2)] # the signal, without noise itp_x = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact) # interpolates the points dx_x = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact, derivative = (1, 0)) # ∂/∂x of the same fit ii_x = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact, derivative = (-1, -1)) # ∫∫ from the corner box = (0.2, 0.7, 0.3, 0.8) # x₁, x₂, y₁, y₂ of a box inside the domain boxint(F, x1, x2, y1, y2) = F(x2, y2) - F(x1, y2) - F(x2, y1) + F(x1, y1) # inclusion–exclusion itp_x(0.4, 0.6), dx_x(0.4, 0.6), boxint(ii_x, box...) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.33773158915965074, 0.39390938114123014, 0.09642290688862255) ``` ::: ::: | | f(0.4, 0.6) | ∂f/∂x (0.4, 0.6) | ∫∫ over the box | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | from the fit | 0.33773159 | 0.39390938 | 0.09642291 | | exact | 0.33773159 | 0.39390943 | 0.09642291 | ``` {.julia .cell-code} viol = maximum(abs(itp_x(p[1], p[2]) - v) for (p, v) in zip(eachcol(pts2), vals2)) # the fit at the points @printf("The largest deviation of the interpolant from the data at the points is %.1e.\n", viol) ``` The largest deviation of the interpolant from the data at the points is 4.0e-13. ## Clustered points and adaptive grids An exact fit needs the grid to separate the points: two points in one grid cell cannot both be matched. A uniform grid sized from the mean density cannot do that for clustered points, and the fit says so with a warning and returns the least-squares fit instead. `grid = :adaptive` places the knots of each axis at the quantiles of the points' coordinates, so a dense band of points gets a dense band of knots — and where the points are dense because the function varies fast there, as in a measurement campaign that samples a layer closely, the dense knots are also where the accuracy is needed: ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} layer(x) = tanh(40x) # a steep layer at the centre u = range(-1, 1, length = 60) xs = sign.(u) .* abs.(u) .^ 2 # 60 points, clustered towards the layer pts1 = reshape(xs, 1, :) # as a 1 × n matrix ys = layer.(xs) # trusted values ku, vu, viol_u = fit_scattered(pts1, ys; mode = :exact) # uniform grid: warns ka, va, viol_a = fit_scattered(pts1, ys; mode = :exact, grid = :adaptive) # adaptive grid itp_u = convolution_interpolation(ku, vu; kernel = :b5, bc = :poly) # the kernel the fit used itp_a = convolution_interpolation(ka, va; kernel = :b5); # a nonuniform grid: the nonuniform :b5 kernel ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
┌ Warning: fit_scattered (:exact): constraint violation 0.009372166006149374 did not reach machine precision. The system may be overdetermined for this grid (try a larger gridsize/oversample) or the data may contain duplicated points with conflicting values. Result is the least-squares fit. If the points are clustered, `grid = :adaptive` places the knots where the points are, so that each point gets its own knot spacing.

``` ::: ::: ::: | | uniform grid | adaptive grid | knots at the points | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | knots | 97 | 97 | 60 | | largest deviation at the points | 9.4e-03 | 1.8e-13 | 0.0e+00 | | largest error against the function | 9.9e-03 | 1.3e-04 | 9.3e-04 | ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Exactness at the points and accuracy between them are different things. On the same clustered points sampled from a function that is smooth everywhere, the uniform fit's least-squares compromise is as accurate as the adaptive fit's exact match, often more so, because the uniform grid spends its knots evenly where the function needs them evenly. The adaptive grid pays off when the points are dense where the function is steep, or when the values themselves must be reproduced. The last column of the table is the nonuniform kernel with its knots at the points — the plain interpolant through the same samples. The fit is more accurate than that as well: among the grids that match the points it takes the smoothest, and the knots it has between the points serve that end. An adaptive grid is nonuniform, so the interpolant on it is the nonuniform one of the [nonuniform page](nonuniform.qmd): derivatives are available, antiderivatives are not. The spacing ratio of adjacent knots is capped by the `ratio` keyword, which keeps the nonuniform kernels well conditioned; raise it for strongly graded data. The grid is still a tensor product, so it helps when the point density is roughly separable along the axes — a boundary layer, a log-scaled axis — and not for isolated clusters. ## Knots and points Two keywords size the grid. `oversample` is the number of knots per mean point spacing, with mode-dependent defaults (lower for `:smooth`, where the penalty does the regularising; higher for `:exact` in two or more dimensions, where random points share cells more often); `gridsize` fixes the knot count outright. Both modes warn when the grid is the limit: `:exact` when the points could not all be matched, `:smooth` when the fitted smoothing would need a finer grid than the budget allows. The [scattered-data benchmark](../benchmarks/scattered.qmd) has the convergence of both modes with the point count, and timings.
